title: The Mantis and the Eland
summary: A dreamer of the old Karoo hears how ǀKaggen the Mantis shaped the first eland from earth, honey and the last of the day, and why it must be met with care.
moral: What is shaped with wonder deserves to be met with wonder.
attribution: A traditional San / Khoikhoi tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A great eland standing in low golden dunes before a pale sun, a small mantis on a rock nearby

sentences.text: Long before the cattle came, when the country was a wide brown sea of sand and thorn, ǀKaggen the Mantis was walking.
He walked on his four thin legs with his head turned to one side, because he was always listening for something interesting.
In a hollow beside a dry pan he found a little earth, and a little honey, and the pale light that the sun leaves on the stones at evening.
“I am in the mood to make something,” he said, and he began to work.
He worked the way the Mantis always worked: quickly, and with a great deal of interest in the result.
He pressed the earth into a shape.
He gave it a long neck, and a proud chest, and horns that turned like the branches of a young tree.
He breathed on it, and it became warm.
“Get up,” he said.
“You are the eland.”
The eland stood up.
It was the most beautiful creature the Mantis had ever seen, and the Mantis was so pleased that he sat down and looked at it for the rest of the day.
He called it by name, and the name was a sound like rain.
The other animals came to the edge of the pan to look, and even they were quiet.
Word of the eland travelled.
The people came from far places to see it, and a young hunter named ǂXo decided that such an animal would make him famous.
He took his bow and followed the eland into the dunes.
The Mantis saw him going and grew afraid.
“Do not hurry,” he told the hunter.
“That creature was not made to be taken by whoever is quickest.
It was made to be seen.
If you would hunt it, learn its ways first.”
ǂXo did not listen at once.
He followed the eland for three days, and each evening he found that it had moved in a wide, slow circle and had not gone far at all.
It grazed where the first green shoots came up after the rain, and its tracks always led back towards the water.
It never hurried, and it never hid.
On the fourth morning the eland stood on a rise and looked at him.
ǂXo put down his bow.
He could not say afterwards why he did it.
He only knew that the animal was too beautiful to be killed for a boast, and that a thing so beautiful was not his to waste.
The Mantis came out from behind a bush.
“Now you have learned something,” he said.
“The eland was made for the people, but only for those who approach it with respect.
It is a creature of the rain, and the rain is not anyone’s servant.”
So the people learned the old ways of the eland: when to follow, when to wait, which parts to use and which to leave, and how to speak of the animal afterwards with thanks.
The Mantis watched them from a stone and nodded, the way an old teacher nods when the lesson has finally arrived.
Children were taught to watch for the eland at first light, when the herds came down to drink and the mist lay along the ground.
They were told not to shout, not to point, and not to run at it.
“Let it see you seeing it,” the old people said.
“Then you will know whether you have understood anything at all.”

Some of the old people say that the eland was the first of all creatures, and that when you see one standing in the low light, you are seeing something that was once made out of earth and honey and the last of the day.
They say you should look at it for a long time.
That is why the old people do not speak loudly of the eland.
A creature made with wonder deserves to be met with wonder, and the one who sees it well has more than the one who takes it.
